Model catalog, picker and usage counters

Native picker selection, Codex subscription counters, model changes inside a loaded chat, and how Codex 2 rows borrow the native catalog.

About 18 min read · 6 sections

On this page
01 Native picker selection 02 Codex subscription counters 03 Chat naming and active-step model switching 04 Mid-turn model changes from the picker 05 Native chats keep their model 06 Codex 2 rows and the native catalog

Part of the Codex app-server adapter.

Native picker selection

nativeModelPicker in the gateway configuration optionally lists the exact native model IDs offered in the desktop picker:

{
  "nativeModelPicker": [
    "gpt-6-astra",
    "gpt-6.1-sol",
    "gpt-5.6-terra",
    "gpt-6-luna"
  ]
}

nativeModelPickerPlacement controls where those native rows appear. The app's Connections → Native GPT fallback models control offers the same choices:

Value Picker behavior
first Native rows before gateway groups; the default when omitted.
last Native rows after gateway groups, keeping fallback visible.
hidden Native rows omitted from the normal picker, not disabled.

For example, add "nativeModelPickerPlacement": "last" alongside the existing model selection. Neither placement nor hiding changes the allowlist itself. With includeHidden: true, hidden native rows are still returned with hidden: true; gateway aliases and their relative order are unchanged. Pagination applies after selection and placement. Existing native chats, explicit native model requests, account defaults and native classification continue to use the full native catalog. No automatic model or account failover is introduced. Use last rather than hidden to keep fallback easy to reach.

This preference belongs to the local execution host's adapter, including a client-only Mac using a shared inference gateway. It does not edit that shared gateway's provider order or credentials. SSH chats use the remote execution host's preference. When running without the gateway adapter, these picker preferences have no effect on the stock native catalog.

Omitting nativeModelPicker retains every native row before placement is applied. Its list must contain 1–256 unique model IDs. Selection applies only to native rows returned by model/list, before combined pagination; gateway aliases are unaffected. With includeHidden: true, excluded native rows remain available with hidden: true. Vendor-hidden rows are never made visible. This is a picker preference, not permission to use or rebind a model: existing native chats, explicit model requests, subagents and native/gateway classification retain the full catalog and their saved choices. The adapter does not edit native authentication, configuration or model-cache files. Registered adapters re-read only these native presentation settings when the picker requests its list; invalid or unreadable changes retain the last valid presentation. Older adapters need normal idle adoption or reconnection to load this reader. Loaded chats keep their own model and account.

The example lists the four models available during the October 23 check. It does not automatically select a newer release or invent a missing family. Update the IDs after checking that account's current catalog.

Verify the picker against the signed native SDK without copying authentication or sending inference:

node scripts/e2e-native-picker.mjs --code /absolute/package \
  --catalog "$HOME/.codex/models_cache.json" --root /tmp/fresh-picker-check

The fixture uses an isolated home, verifies the four selected rows plus a gateway row and hidden discovery, and checks that the public catalog remains unchanged.

Codex subscription counters

The gateway records Codex counters only when the Codex subscription backend itself sends them: the default numeric headers x-codex-primary-* and x-codex-secondary-* (used-percent, window-minutes, reset-at), read on successful and failed (for example 429) replies, and codex.rate_limits stream events for the default codex family. Events that name another limit are ignored so they are never mislabelled. A window is kept only when all three of its values are valid (used-percent finite from 0 to 100, window-minutes a positive integer, reset-at an epoch second in a sensible range); nothing is inferred, filled in or coerced from null, booleans, or text. Other Responses API providers never produce Codex rows. A failure of the observer cannot fail or retry the request.

No percentages are available when the backend omits them. At the time of writing the live backend answers a request with HTTP 200 and response.completed but sends no numeric quota headers or rate events, so a live gateway currently shows no Codex row. This feature does not add a backend endpoint and does not claim parity with the native Codex quota; it only shows counters the backend has reported.

A counter belongs to the credential file the request ran with. Each request records the file's identity (device, inode, size, modification and change times, mode, and that it is readable; never its content or a token) before and after its token is read, and the write checks it again. A different path, a replaced or rewritten file, a permissions change, or a file the gateway cannot read leaves no counters, including after a restart. A credential refresh during a request also drops that request's counters; the next request records them.

When the desktop reads account/rateLimits/read, the adapter adds known rejected Claude windows to rateLimitsByLimitId with separate gateway: IDs. A rejected window establishes 100% usage. Allowed events do not establish a percentage and are not rendered as invented zero usage. A Codex row is added as gateway:<providerId>:codex, labelled Codex · <providerId>, with primary and secondary exactly as observed. A window that has already reset is shown as null, and a row with no live window is omitted. Observations older than 24 hours or more than five minutes in the future are omitted until new provider data arrives. Native rateLimits, account identity, usage permission, credits, upsell fields, and native map entries retain their values. A gateway outage leaves the native response usable. The installed app's rendering of additional usage rows still requires a desktop check. Usage updates never modify the model catalog or create another executor generation.

gateway codex-shim --config /absolute/path/gateway.local.json \
  --codex /absolute/path/original-codex -- app-server --listen stdio://

Stdout carries JSON-RPC only. The adapter forwards notifications, maps server request IDs for approvals, bounds frames to 16 MiB, and stops its child on exit. Non-server commands, including --version, pass through unchanged. The adapter accepts stdio:// and private unix:// listeners. A Unix listener serves the WebSocket protocol used by desktop SSH connections. A listener started with --ssh, which gives it a gateway control home, retires itself once a newer release is installed and it holds no session; the next connection then starts it on the installed release. A listener started with a custom --listen unix://PATH, which has no control home, keeps its previous behavior: it does not exit on its own after an install. The adapter gives each connection its own native connection. Gateway executors are shared when the unified service has shared execution enabled; legacy installations keep per-connection executors. It refuses occupied sockets, requires a user-owned directory without group/world write access, and sets the socket to mode 0600. Network WebSocket listeners are rejected.

For the desktop SSH path, install the managed command on the remote Mac:

gateway ssh register --codex /opt/homebrew/bin/codex
gateway ssh status

Use the absolute path returned by command -v codex before registration. The managed ~/.local/bin/codex command decorates app-server operations and delegates other commands to that original CLI. Registration refuses an unrelated existing command. gateway ssh unregister moves only its own command to Trash. Native configuration and authentication files are unchanged.

The app prepends ~/.local/bin to the remote command search path and starts a Unix listener. The managed command uses a gateway-owned control home under ~/.local/state/gw-ssh, scoped to the gateway configuration and native home. It redirects only the original app-server proxy child's control home to that socket. Inference and account discovery retain the original native home. Codex's own daemon socket is not replaced. A live gateway listener is reused; a crashed socket is recovered only when its private ownership record matches. A bootstrap that finds a swap cut off halfway by a crash (the record names a new listener that never took over the address) restores the previous record and continues, so a crash never leaves SSH refused. Under the same lock it removes dead private .gw-* sockets and links and stale lease temp files, only in the managed gw-ssh folder or during a replacement, never for a custom --listen path. Add the host under Settings, Connections, SSH, then select its workspace. The built-in Control other devices connection reaches the native engine directly and bypasses a desktop or SSH wrapper. The separate native transport adapter reuses the machine's original registration and routes that connection through the same gateway router. Its rendered checks are still in progress on the test Mac.

Chat naming and active-step model switching

The client owns chat naming. The adapter forwards native thread/name/set, saved-title reads, and live name notifications; it adds no title tool or naming instructions. Caller-supplied dynamic tools remain unchanged. Read-only saved-chat metadata needs neither gateway inference nor model discovery.

Choose a gateway model in a new chat. A loaded chat cannot switch between native and gateway providers in this Codex version. The adapter rejects that change before inference. Switching Claude and Codex 2 inside a gateway chat works because they share the gateway provider and its account-scoped replay handling. Native return from gateway history is not supported: a real probe failed on foreign item IDs. The adapter does not rewrite stored native history to bypass it.

Gateway executors enable Codex's active-step model switching. The adapter forwards thread/settings/update, turn/settings/update, turn/steer, and goal operations with their original turn IDs and authorization fields. A thread-level model selection remains the default after a saved chat resumes. An active-turn model update applies at the next inference step, unless the destination differs in node_repl or review settings: the SDK then rejects it, as natively, and the adapter forwards the error (which rows). A captured tool step keeps its approval requirements; changing thread access updates subsequent turns.

These controls passed live tests with Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Codex 2 GPT-6.1-Sol, which were then in one node_repl group; only adapter tests cover a rejected switch. Goal creation, reads, updates, notifications, and clearing were tested. scripts/e2e-goal-switch.mjs checks automatic goal continuation with real inference in an isolated native home: an active goal whose chat switches gateway model mid-goal with thread/settings/update, as the picker does, must start its next turn by itself and send that turn's requests on the new model. Every rendered control remains a separate desktop check.

Mid-turn model changes from the picker

The desktop picker changes a model only with thread/settings/update, so the running turn finishes on its old model. With "midTurnModelSwitch": true in the gateway configuration (off when absent), the adapter also offers an applied picker change to a running gateway turn on another model. It sends one turn/settings/update with only the model and that turn's ID, after the thread update succeeded:

  1. The thread update is always forwarded first, so the next turn, a resume and a fork use the new model whatever happens to the offer.
  2. The tokenizer recount runs for every active-turn model change, including ones a CLI or script sends. A history the new model cannot hold is refused before anything reaches the SDK.
  3. The SDK's own active-step check decides the review groups (which rows); the adapter keeps no copy of them.

An applied offer takes effect at the next inference step and is recorded as model_switch_promoted. A refusal from either check, an unapplied answer or any error is recorded as model_switch_deferred with reason (context, review_group, not_applied or error). It is never reported to the desktop: the picker change already succeeded and applies from the next turn, as without the setting. Nothing is offered to an idle chat, a turn already on that model, a throwaway fork, a native chat or a turn this connection did not start. A switch to or from Claude starts a new Claude CLI session, which costs one cache write. The desktop may show the new model while the running turn's earlier steps used the old one. Only adapter tests cover the offer so far; a rendered desktop check is still required before this becomes the default. Changing the setting needs a fresh adapter connection.

Native chats keep their model

The adapter never changes a native chat's model or provider. When "Authenticated workspace changed" restarts the desktop's local engine, ChatGPT 26.1007.71326 resumes each open chat with model: null and modelProvider: null. The signed SDK then restores the model, provider and reasoning effort saved with the chat. It skips that restore when the request names a model or a provider, or carries a config.model or config.model_reasoning_effort key, and then runs the configured default model. The adapter therefore forwards such a resume unchanged. A native fork never takes its parent's model: it runs the model it names or the configured default, so a fork that names no model, such as a side chat, is forwarded unchanged as well.

The adapter adds nothing to a native chat's request. thread/resume, thread/fork, turn/start and the settings updates reach the SDK exactly as the desktop sent them: the adapter never adds or changes model, modelProvider, config.model or config.model_reasoning_effort. A fork that names the chat's model without an effort therefore gets the SDK's own effort, as it does natively. Gateway chats are different: the SDK cannot restore a gateway alias, so the adapter still restores a gateway chat's reasoning (compaction), and only gateway chats are written to that reasoning store. Releases 0.3.9 and 0.4.0 added the saved effort to the desktop's resume, whose null model is no override, so after every engine restart a chat on GPT-6.1-Sol came back on the configured default model with its saved effort. Release 0.4.1 first limited that to requests naming the chat's model and now removes it, so the reasoning_restored event no longer reports provider: native.

The signed SDK (0.162.0-alpha.17.2) with a localhost mock upstream confirmed both rules: the desktop's resume kept GPT-6.1-Sol, and the same resume with an added effort returned the configured default. A fork that named no model ran the configured default whether or not it carried an effort. scripts/e2e-native-model.mjs requires the adapter to give every desktop shape the same model and effort as the SDK gives it directly.

Gateway sub-agents on native rows

A gateway executor can spawn a Codex 2 or Claude sub-agent whose saved model is a native catalog slug such as gpt-6.1-sol. That child remains a gateway chat: its saved provider stays gatefox (subscription_gateway if saved before 1.8.0) or, on an opted-in Mac, openai, and the adapter routes reads, history, interrupts, turns and resumes to the executor that owns it. A resume with no model or reasoning override lets the SDK restore its saved state. The child's web search settings are forwarded as the caller saved them, as on gateway aliases: the adapter no longer forces web_search off, because the Codex route forwards the hosted tool and every other route drops it. If an explicit model/provider or a config.model or config.model_reasoning_effort key opens the SDK's restore gate without selecting a different child, the adapter repeats the child's saved native model and provider. It recovers an unspecified effort only from the child's saved reasoning record, rollout, or thread metadata; it never invents a launch default or replaces a caller-supplied effort. A conflicting model or provider is refused.

This is deliberately not a general native-to-gateway model switch. The adapter allows it only when the backend's saved child metadata records a parent, returns the requested thread id, classifies as a gateway child in this adapter, and its actual current model equals the requested native slug. The frozen executor applies this same check to config.model. Another native model, an unknown alias, a mismatched rollout record, or a parent-shaped native child is still refused.

Codex 2 rows and the native catalog

Codex 2 rows serve the same models as native Codex, so the desktop adapter gives them the harness half of the native row. Each Codex 2 row in the public catalog names its upstream model in upstream_slug. The adapter looks that slug up in the local native catalog it loaded at startup and copies these fields:

  • model_messages: the base prompt (instructions_template) and Codex's other model messages, together with include_skills_usage_instructions, include_plugin_usage_instructions and include_apps_usage_instructions. Native GPT-6.1-Sol turns all three off because its template already holds that guidance. With the gateway's own true values Codex repeated it: with skills alone, 2,554 characters (about 550 input tokens) on every request. Without a native template the gateway values stay;
  • tool_mode, apply_patch_tool_type and shell_type;
  • the default_reasoning_level, default_verbosity and default_reasoning_summary defaults, and support_verbosity. A default effort the route does not offer is not copied;
  • effective_context_window_percent and truncation_policy;
  • context_window, but only when the native value is at or below the upstream's max_context_window. Otherwise, or when the upstream reports no maximum, the upstream window stays;
  • node_repl_disabled, node_repl_auto_review_required, guardian, auto_review_model_override, requires_sandboxed_review (data only: no SDK reads it) and model_specialty (node_repl).

Everything else keeps the upstream value: service tiers, multi-agent fields, the window maximum, the auto-compaction limit, input modalities and reasoning levels. comp_hash is never copied. supports_search_tool is on for a Codex 2 row only when its provider bridges tool search ("toolSearch": "bridge") and the native row has it on. Otherwise it stays off: the ChatGPT backend refuses a tool_search tool that the gateway forwards, so without the bridge the gateway drops it on that route (details). The hosted web_search tool is a separate setting and is on there: the adapter copies the native row's web_search_tool_type, so a Codex 2 chat sends that tool exactly as native Codex does and the Codex route forwards it. A slug without a native row, and every Claude, Copilot or other row, loses the field -- those routes cannot run hosted search and the gateway drops the tool (details). Every row otherwise stays as the gateway published it (tool search off unless bridged), apart from the strictest native node_repl policy and the native confirmation and classifier texts (node_repl). The rows the adapter builds drop upstream_slug. At each launch the native-catalog preflight first writes desktop-models.json with the plain gateway rows, marker included; the adapter replaces that file with the copied rows on its first successful cache restore or host refresh, and every gateway chat start refreshes first. Codex 0.160.0 and the gateway SDK both ignore the marker, as they do in the plain catalog that CLI and remote clients read. Those clients have no native catalog, so they keep the gateway rows unchanged.

The inference host still never supplies instructions. The offline cache stores only the host's public rows; the adapter rebuilds the copy from the native catalog on every start, and a changed native row changes the catalog revision, which starts a new executor generation for new chats.

Code mode runs in a separate codex-code-mode-host process that Codex starts from beside its own executable. The gateway SDK package ships that companion and records its digest in the build receipt as codeModeHostSha256; the execution host enables Code Mode only after that verified receipt. A host file the receipt does not name, or one whose bytes differ from it, fails the whole SDK's verification, as any other changed component does. When the installed package has a gateway SDK whose receipt names no host (a package built before the companion shipped), the adapter keeps the gateway's direct tool mode and still copies the other fields. Without a gateway SDK, executors run the desktop's own Codex and take the native code mode. The same rule covers the native rows that the executor catalog carries for sub-agents naming a model directly (a role's model, default_subagent_model or Ultra delegation): without the host those rows get direct tools in executors, so their commands run instead of failing with "failed to spawn code-mode host". Those carried rows have the search flag off, as the Codex 2 rows do: a bare model name resolves to the Codex subscription route, which drops tool_search because the ChatGPT backend refuses it. No provider can take that name first, because a gateway model alias spelled exactly like a native slug is refused whenever the adapter loads the gateway catalog, at launch and at each refresh, against the native slugs it read at launch; a native model that appears later is checked at the next launch. (Before 0.4.4 every such sub-agent request failed with unsupported_tool.) The native engine keeps its own catalog unchanged.

The executable selected for each new executor generation decides whether Code Mode is available; the adapter does not reuse that decision from the package that opened the desktop connection. A recovered SDK without the companion host gives every gateway and carried native row an explicit tool_mode: "direct", including rows whose native metadata omitted or named an unknown mode. Direct mode overrides Code Mode feature flags. It preserves node_repl, permissions, review and instructions, and never changes the native engine's catalog.

Every gateway row publishes max_context_window: the provider's own maximum when it reports one, otherwise the row's window. Without it a row inherited Codex's global cap of 872K, which cut Claude's 1M window.

Gateway executor homes link the native AGENTS.md, agents, skills, plugins, hooks.json and prompts, so client hooks (for example memory hooks) and saved prompts work in gateway chats as in native ones. Authentication and config.toml are never linked.

The executor home's config.toml snapshot writes bare keys (notify = …) wherever TOML allows them, and quotes only keys that need it. Tools that edit config.toml line by line, such as the Computer Use installer, look for a bare notify = and append their own when they miss a quoted "notify" =. That left two root notify keys and the engine failed with duplicate key on resume (30 Oct 2026). A shared generation keeps its snapshot across restarts, so on reuse the gateway also drops the earlier of two single-line root assignments to the same key; the later line is the newer intent. Tables and multi-line values are left alone.

On 13 Oct 2026 a low-effort GPT-6.1-Sol turn through a development gateway sent the native 21,769-character base prompt as a developer message (Responses lite has no top-level instructions). With Codex 0.160.0 the model called the code-mode exec tool; with the gateway SDK and the copied direct mode it called exec_command. Both turns completed, and the second request of each turn read 97-98% of its input from the cache. Native and upstream both reported GPT-6.1-Sol at 500K that day, so its window did not change.

A resumed chat keeps the base instructions saved with it, as natively; chats started before this change keep their empty base prompt. When it starts a new gateway chat without a saved preference, the adapter still selects medium effort and auto summaries, so the native default shows in the model list but does not yet start the chat. Those defaults never replace an existing chat's settings on resume; the chat's own reasoning is restored instead, as described above.

node_repl (browser, Chrome and computer use)

Gateway rows get the native node_repl policy, and rows with no native counterpart always require review. The gateway serves the reviewer codex-auto-review through the Codex subscription for every Auto-review approval in a gateway executor, not only node_repl; 0.3.9 declined them, and their context now leaves the chat's own provider. The rules, evidence and fail-closed cases are only in node_repl on gateway rows.
